newsitem.title: BOSNIA: No arms delivery till Bosnia Moslems sack aide - US.
newsitem.headline: No arms delivery till Bosnia Moslems sack aide - US.

text.p: American weapons for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation will stay aboard a ship in a Croatian port until the Moslem side fires a defence official seen as close to Iran, the U.S. said on Friday.
A chartered freighter carrying the bulk of a $100 million arms shipment for the federation docked in the port of Ploce in neighbouring Croatia on Thursday and unloading was to have started on Friday.

But Clinton administration officials disclosed in Washington a few hours later that the tanks, guns and helicopters would not be unloaded until Bosnia's government dismissed deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic.
"There is a delay in the offload of the ship," a U.S. official connected with the "Train and Equip" programme for Bosnia's fledgling post-war federal army told Reuters in Ploce.

"There are issues that are being discussed with the Bosnian government. There has been a meeting with President (Alija) Izetbegovic. We just waiting to see if the government can meet our wishes over next few days," he said.
"It has assured us it will take those steps. In the meantime, the cargo will remain aboard the ship under U.S. control. The ship may have to pull away from the pier because of port regulations."
U.S. Embassy officials in Sarajevo said the head of a Train and Equip programme which supplies the armaments, Ambassador James Pardew, was discussing the issue with Bosnian leaders.
"There are number of issues to be resolved and discussions are currently on the way," embassy spokesman Bill Richey said.
Richey declined to go into details on what other issues there may be apart from Cengic's removal but confirmed that the shipment will not be unloaded until the issues are resolved.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the equipment would be sent on to storage sites in Bosnia only when "steps needed to promote cooperation in forming the joint armed forces in the Federation" had been taken.

Burns did not specify the issues at stake. But a senior administration official said Washington was concerned about Cengic, a Moslem nationalist with links to Iran, and strained relations with Croat partners in the shaky federation.

Cengic himself said in Sarajevo on October 8 that the United States was pressing for his removal after the Washington Post reported he was trying to undermine the Train and Equip programme as a client of Iran.

The U.S. equipment includes 45 M-60 battle tanks, 80 M-11 armoured personnel carriers, 15 UH-1H helicopters, 840 light anti-tank weapons, 45,000 M-16 rifles and ammunition. The programme also includes instruction for Federation army troops.

The programme was devised in Dayton, Ohio last November as part of the successful Bosnia peace talks to ensure a post-war parity of forces in the region and help the federation army counter any future threat from its Serb foes.

European powers oppose Washington's patronage of Moslem-Croat forces, saying it undermines diplomatic goals to promote reconciliation and arms control in Bosnia, divided by the Dayton peace accord into the Federation and a Serb entity.

The Moslem-led Bosnian army was outgunned by Serb forces during a 43-month war in the Balkan republic and had to rely on Islamic countries such as Iran for arms shipments, which violated an international arms embargo on former Yugoslavia.
